utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To inform the parties, the late start allowed us to start in a fully-composed Bench rather than to rely on 15 bis. I do understand that Mr. Emmerson is suffering a delay in arriving in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could offer sincere apologies on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not blame Mr. Emmerson himself for delays of aeroplanes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And also to apologise for him having to enter the courtroom during the first session perhaps while the witness is already testifying and wanted to express gratitude for the indication, I think, Your Honours, that cross-examination of this witness will not commence until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Other matters could be dealt with at the end of the day, time permitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber intends to start with the witness's examination-in-chief and then if there's any time left today that we'd then perhaps already spend some time on the rather long list of exhibits marked for identification, some of them for quite understandable reasons, but to see whether we can clean that list a bit. Mr. Re, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I do understand that the next witness there are -- there is no application for protective measures, and your next witness would be Rrustem Tetaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, there is no application for protective measures from the Prosecution, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to be sure. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Brahimaj is not receiving the translation in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then is he on the right channel? Then I ask the assistance of the technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And is the volume such that -- does he receive it in any other language. Of course, I should continue to speak to see whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Apparently it is coming through on a channel that he hasn't previously been using, but he's got it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a witness in respect of whom the Prosecution has foreshadowed making application under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And we provided the Trial Chamber and the Defence with a copy of the proposed statement on the 19th of April giving notice of our intention to use it. We've heard nothing from the Defence up until now as to whether there was any opposition to that course. And we'd make the formal application to rely upon those 38 paragraphs in that statement signed on the 17th of April which are basically an extract of the 106, I think, paragraphs of the consolidated statement of the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any objection against admission of the 38-paragraph witness statement where it says that it is the 13th and 17th of April of this year statement, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The date of signature, I think, is the 17th of April, that's why I used that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes it is a bit confusing because on the front page of the statement you find all kind of dates, but it is a statement which on the second page starts with paragraph 1, "Since 1981 the regime in Belgrade," that's the first few -- the first line of page 2, continuing up to and including what I would expect to be page 20 because it follows page 19, although page 20 is not -- is not numbered. Then there is a -- another signature on a page which is numbered 12, which is quite surprising after 20, which is the certification of the interpreter. Mr. Re, is that -- because that's dated also the 17th of April, and the witness acknowledgement and the signatures on every page is also 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, it bears -- the signature date is the 17th of April, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Just in order to avoid whatever further confusion, the stamped number on the top is U1 -- U0160890 up to and -- yes. Yes, it says O1 -- U0160901 and I'm just now trying to reconcile myself how 890 plus 20 makes 901. There must be something --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've just checked with Mr. Dixon and Mr. Harvey, and we are operating off an entirely different document. We're operating off a document with a number of U0160848. I've been through rapidly a variety of places where I would find the document that has been referred to and I don't seem to have a copy of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before we continue, Mr. Guy-Smith, perhaps it would be more polite to say -- to ask the witness first to give his solemn declaration. Good afternoon. Welcome in this courtroom. I apologise for continuing our conversation where you entered the courtroom and we apparently did not pay the appropriate attention to your arrival, Mr. Tetaj, because I take it that you are Mr. Tetaj. Mr. Tetaj, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Before I invite you to make that solemn declaration, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the text of the solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Before we start your examination, Mr. Tetaj, I'd like to clarify a matter with the parties. So if you would have one moment for us. I do understand that the pages you're referring to, Mr. Guy-Smith, are the pages of the full statement given by the witness and put on paper on the 17th of April, which is a document containing 100 paragraphs and that the Prosecution has selected 38 paragraphs, mainly coming from this statement, Mr. Re, as far as I understand, and has sent that as the proposed 92 ter statement to the parties on the 19th of April of 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what I understand the representation of being, and I have no reason to disbelieve it, but there seems to be some slippage because we're not finding that document and I have been operating off of the document that I referred to just now. I'm -- I'm having it double-checked as we speak -- actually, it's triple-checked. Perhaps I missed it, but I don't seem to find this document in any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see, as a matter of fact, I see an e-mail by Mr. Re to, among others, Gregor Guy-Smith, the 19th of April, 8.20 p.m., which starts with: "Witnesses for the week of the 23rd of April." And then at the end it says: "Attached is a signed proposed Rule 92 ter statement for part of Rrustem Tetaj's evidence. The witness signed a larger consolidated statement on the 17th of April, which will be -- we will forward to the Defence counsel tomorrow. The proposed 92 ter statement is an extract from that larger statement." Now, I see that attached to that e-mail was a 92 ter statement which --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- gives the numbers and -- U0160878 up to U0161 -- 0901.tif. That's what I understand. That gives me the impression that it was sent to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It has just been -- it has just been found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I said, there might have been some slippage, which is why I said I certainly didn't accuse Mr. Re of not doing anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- they claim to have done. There seems to be some slippage. If we could have a moment, we will be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that one is just an extract of the other with a lot of details and some elements not contained in the 92 ter statement. So I think if you prepared on the basis of the larger one, then it would not cause you major problems. Mr. Re -- but first, Mr. Tetaj, I again have to apologise, but we had to clarify this issue before we could start your examination. You'll first be examined by Mr. Re, who's -- yes, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just clarify for the record that there is no objection on the part of Mr. Haradinaj to this application being made, but I would request that the full requirements of the rule, Rule 92 ter, in particular subparagraph (a)(ii), be clarified with the witness in the following way: That it is confirmed that the witness is going to be available after the statement has been admitted for questioning and cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- I mean, 92 ter is -- includes that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I only raise that, Your Honour, because there was an issue over his attendance and hence the need for a subpoena, which was issued. So I'm just guarding against the situation where the statement may be admitted and no further questions may be put to the witness because he is right to introduce -- could that just be clarified. That's all I ask, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, are you ready to start your examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take a similar position, having just rapidly reviewed the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm in the same situation, Your Honour; I take the same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we could not decide even on admission until we have gone through the formalities of 92 ter. That's the reason why I did not yet invite you at this stage to express yourself because we still need the witness to attest to certain matters. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tetaj. Your name is Rrustem Tetaj?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were you born on the 27th of April, 1953, in Donja Luka in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were you a -- were you living in Strumica, Macedonia, from 1978 to 1998 -- sorry, 1999 as a member of the JNA, the JNA barracks in Strumica?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you graduate in 1978 from the military academy at the JNA in Zadar as a second lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And from 1987 were you a deputy commander of artillery at the JNA barracks in Strumica until you became a first-class captain in 1989?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I do not fully remember what you said, but looking at the transcript, page 8, line 20, you corrected 1998, but it now reads 1999 where I suppose it should read 1989. Could you please verify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Tetaj, you were living in the JNA barracks from 1978 to 1989. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And to summarize, were -- did you leave the JNA in December, 1989 because you were forced to do so, in effect, because you were an ethnic Albanian JNA officer and the JNA Supreme Command was eliminating ethnic Albanian officers and soldiers from the JNA because of tensions the Yugoslav authorities were encountering in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you a statement. I'm going to hand it to you --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: That's exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to hand you a handwritten statement of some 12 pages with your signature on it dated the 17th of April, 2007. And it is 65 ter number 1328, for the record. What I want you to do is just to read through that document, please, and just read it -- read it through -- just read it through to yourself for a moment, and I understand you have a copy of it -- or you were given a copy of it after you signed it. You don't need to take your copy out if you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Re, are you now referring to a document we don't have before us, as you said "handwritten document."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did I say "handwritten"? I apologise. I meant to say "signed statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just look through the statement. Does it bear your signature on each page? Is it the statement you made to the Prosecution on the 17th of April, 2007?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is it true and correct, what is written in the statement which you signed?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I believe so. There are things which are exactly as said, there are also things about which I have heard. So if I would be given the possibility from the Judges here. At first I'd like to clarify my position. Is that possible, honourable Judges?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, at this very moment we are identifying what your statement was, and the Chamber is aware that you have made --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's -- I just would like to ask you to clarify my position, just as you told me so. You didn't give me time. Could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, if at the end of your testimony there's anything you would like to add or you think is important for us to know, we'll give you an opportunity to add anything. But at this very moment the only thing we are doing is that we look at your statement because we are not going to ask you to repeat everything you said in that statement. Then Mr. Re will ask you additional questions perhaps on matters which are not contained in that statement or to clarify certain matters that are in that statement. And if at the very end you think that there is some important matter we have not heard of and which you think we should hear about, then we'll give you an opportunity to do that so -- but we'll first give an opportunity to Mr. Re to ask questions. And then at the end we'll give you an opportunity to add. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, this has not to do with the statement but with my coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was -- I was ordered to come here by all means. I didn't know I should have come directly here; however, there was pressure on the part of the Prosecutor office for me to come here. This is -- this has been also sent to me in written form, so I've come here to clarify the truth, to speak about the truth as much as I know about it. A long time has passed since then, so I'll do my best to speak about things. However, my coming here is against my desire and against my personal will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- you are here because you have been ordered to appear before this Tribunal, Mr. Tetaj. Of course the Chamber is aware because the Chamber issued that order, that's one; and second, you are thus fulfilling your civil obligation to assist this Court in trying to find the truth. Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, if we can just go back to the statement of the 17th of April, and I just wish to get you to clarify for the Trial Chamber that what is in there is true and correct and that you've signed every page of that statement.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On that basis, may I be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection? I take it that it's a combined question that it's -- that the witness has attested that the witness statement reflects his declaration and that the witness would say, if examined the same, if he says it's the truth, whereas he expected to tell us the truth, then we, the Chamber, would be inclined to consider that to be the 92 ter (A)(iii) statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is no objection. I would simply repeat the point I made earlier that the witness confirmed that he will answer questions from all the parties and Your Honours after questions and further questions have been put by Mr. Re. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections on behalf of Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None on behalf of Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, would you please assign a number to the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, I take it that you gave the -- you gave the original to Tetaj. Has he received a translation in his own language?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he's reading off, yes, because I don't think as a matter of fact from this statement the Chamber received a translation. But original English translation looked at by the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have a short summary prepared of this. Does Your Honours wish me to read it on the record now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Also for Mr. Tetaj to know. Mr. Tetaj, from the statement we just spoke about, a summary has been made, because we are not going through all these facts anew, and therefore for the public to know what is in your statement, Mr. Re will read a short summary of what is in the statement. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have a copy of the summary to distribute to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the Defence has --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't seen a copy of this statement before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- usually a copy of the summary is presented to the other party. It's not the evidence to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and if there are any points arising, they can always be corrected at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters kindly ask for a copy of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll provide you with a copy. Yes, you need more than one copy to serve more than one interpreter. It seems that a copy has arrived in each of the four booths, Mr. Re. Therefore please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness is a Kosovar Albanian former JNA officer who left the JNA in 1989. After leaving the JNA, he worked as a teacher in a secondary school until 1992, when he left because of systematic discrimination by the Serbian authorities against Albanian teachers. In 1993 he was arrested and tried by the Serbian authorities for subversive activities. He spent two years in prison. He first heard of the KLA or UCK in 1996 or 1997 through the media. His first encounter with the KLA was at a funeral in late 1997 in Lausa. The witness first found out about the presence of the KLA in the Dukagjin area when the MUP attacked the Haradinaj family compound at the end of March, 1998; before this, some MUP officers had been killed in Ratis and Gllogjan. The witness was in Donja Luka, about 6 kilometres from Gllogjan, when the MUP attacked the Haradinaj compound. He saw air attacks carried out by MUP helicopters. The witness considered his life to be in danger after this because of his former involvement in the JNA, and he left his village. He went to Gllogjan several days after the attack and attended the funeral of some of those killed in the attack. After the MUP withdrew from Gllogjan, local Albanian men controlled the village. Several days after the funeral, he learnt that the KLA had established an organised defence and guard duty in that village. His brother told him of seeing armed soldiers with KLA insignia and of a check-point manned by KLA soldiers from the village. The witness saw a KLA check-point in Gllogjan about a week after the funeral, manned by armed KLA soldiers in camouflage uniform. He went there because it had become known as the epicentre of the KLA. By the beginning of April, 1998 Dubrava, Babaloc, Gramocelj, Shaptej, and Lumbardh had started to form their own KLA village headquarters. The KLA was using doubtful methods to recruit volunteers, such as their soldiers going at night to the houses of those who had not yet joined the KLA and firing rounds after leaving. Mr. Tetaj went to Gllogjan to join the KLA and to discuss the situation because people in his village were awaiting his decision to join the KLA before they would organise themselves. A lot of people were black listed by Faton Mehemetaj and Fitnete Ramosaj for not being loyal to the KLA or for sympathising with the opposition, LDK, or for not having worked for the MUP or other authorities. Lists of their names were circulated among KLA guards, who were to refuse access to the village of those whose names were on the list. Mr. Tetaj's name was on such a list, and at the beginning of May 1998 he was interrogated for two hours by Faton Mehemetaj in Pozar and accused of being a MUP informer before being released. He had not yet joined the KLA then. The witness heard of the kidnapping of several Serbs in the Dukagjin area in May 1998. The FARK had about 500 soldiers in three brigades. It operated separately to the KLA. Each organisation had its own military structure. The brigade commanders were: Nazif Ramabaja in Barane, Shemsedin Cekaj in Zebelj, and Tahir Zemaj in Prapaqan, who was the FARK commander. That completes the summary of what is contained in the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you some further questions about other things which were in your large statement to the Office of the Prosecutor but are not in that statement or the summary I've just read out, Mr. Tetaj. The first thing I'm going to ask you about is your visit to the KLA headquarters in Gllogjan in April, 1998. In your 92 ter statement, paragraphs 19 to 20, you refer to going to KLA headquarters to see the KLA in Gllogjan. Who did you go there with?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I was interested to know after what happened, after the attack on Haradinaj in Gllogjan so due to the situation created in the surrounding villages around Gllogjan. I was interested and curious to go to Gllogjan and to meet with people there, people who might know something or -- our intention was to join the UCK for self-defence; that is, for protecting the people where we lived and the surrounding areas. So I decided to go there. I went there with my brother and my cousin. We were in a car and we travelled during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a check-point in the village when you got there?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was an improvised check-point, very simple kind of check-point. There were three people. One was wearing uniform, the other were not wearing uniform, so that was what we saw there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they KLA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: One of them was wearing a uniform, the others -- I'm not sure. Somebody had some kind of uniform, but I'm not sure what kind of uniform was there -- was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which military organisation did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: It was at the beginning. I didn't know anything about what kind of organisation; however, judging on the place, they were people from the UCK.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did they stop you?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: They stopped us -- I told them -- them that I wanted to meet some people who were competent for the defence of the village. So they stopped us. They asked us, Where do you come from? I told them that I was determined to meet people and talk to them about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, may I just ask one additional question. Mr. Re asked you, Mr. Tetaj, whether at the check-point --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether KLA uniforms -- whether the soldiers were dressed in the KLA uniforms. You said: "One of them was wearing a uniform." Could you tell us what kind of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any insignia on it, any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military uniform. It had an insignia of Kosovo Liberation Army on the arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether any of those soldiers were armed?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They had an automatic rifle. Each of them had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, I believe that the question asked by Mr. Re at this point may be somewhat inaccurate or misleading. He says: "Do you remember whether any of those soldiers were armed?" The evidence we have at present is that one individual was in a uniform and the other two individuals were not in uniform. So I'm not sure that we're in a position yet to make a determination whether anybody other than the one soldier, one individual in a uniform was, in fact, a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, Mr. Re has drawn our attention to paragraph 19 of the 92 ter statement which is in evidence which says it was manned by armed soldiers. So therefore, I think we have sufficient basis in the evidence to put that question to the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they have any communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they had a communication equipment. It was a simple kind of equipment with which they could communicate, yes, they had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? What did they have?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: We call them walkie-talkies, small kind of --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they use that --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: A small kind of equipment. They used it. They used -- they talked on it, then after some minutes they allowed us to move further ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they check your identification before allowing you to go further?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they asked for my ID, to check my identity. They looked at it. Some of them knew me already, so they allowed me to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know who any of the people who stopped you were at the time when you stopped you?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't know any of them, but I heard later that one of them was Daut Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tell the Court about the circumstances in which you heard that one of them was Daut Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: The moment when I saw them, I couldn't recognise any of them. I asked me [as interpreted] but they told me that they knew me. But later I learned that the person who was there was Daut Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you learn that it was Daut Haradinaj? Tell the Court about how you found out it was him.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Later I inquired. I had also my contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you see this person again, if at all, Daut Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember. That's a long time ago, however. Later I saw him. I don't remember where. I'm sure I saw him at a meeting or probably in the streets. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you saw him again, was he wearing a KLA uniform?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Often he did not wear uniform. Sometimes he wore uniform, sometimes he didn't wear a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you allowed to go in the village after you went through this check-point?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I went to the centre of the village. I was received there by somebody, and then he took us to a certain place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the person who received you a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He was a civilian. As far as I remember, he had nothing on [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did he take you to?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He took us through a door. There was a two-storey house. There was a chair inside the house. We sat down and then we waited until we were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whose house was it?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Later, I learned that it was the house of Ismail Haradinaj, that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you waited until you were called. Who called you?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Later we were told to enter inside. There I saw the father of Ramush Haradinaj, Hilmi. I knew him before. We were told to wait more, and then after some time I was called, I don't remember who, then we went up to the second floor and there we met with Ramush and with [indiscernible]. That was the first time we met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "Ramush," do you mean Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you were told to wait. What were you told to wait -- or who were you told to wait for when you were waiting on the chair?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Then the commander came and he took us in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just go back to what I was asking you a moment ago. Who were you told that you were -- or what were you told was the reason why you were waiting there?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: We were told to wait until the commander would come. I don't know exactly what more. I don't know who told us this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware as of that moment who the commander was; that is, when you were sitting there waiting for the commander?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: No, no. No, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you were --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I thought I would meet somebody who was -- who would be well-informed. I would talk to him, but I didn't know exactly who this person would be. We were told he would be the commander; that's how he was addressed to us. I didn't know exactly who the person was. I had no idea who the person would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said after waiting for the commander you were taken upstairs and you met with Ramush Haradinaj. Who was he with?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: We entered the room. We waited a few minutes, then two persons came in afterwards. I did not know any of them before. We greeted each other. We -- I told them that my name was Rrustem Tetaj, that I was a military man, that I had graduated from the army, and that I had come here to discuss about the UCK.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The two people with Ramush Haradinaj, were they KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: No. The -- there were two persons. It was Ramush and Togeri. These were the people who came. I didn't know them before. That's what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniforms, camouflage ones, with boots. One of them carried a cap. They were armed. We talked very briefly. He heard my opinion, then they suggested us what we should do later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which one was wearing the cap, Ramush or Togeri?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Ramush carried a cap. Togeri spoke -- did not say anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the uniforms have the KLA insignia you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: No. I did not hear anything about it. They were just present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll make my question clearer. You referred earlier to KLA insignia, that's patches. Do you remember whether either Ramush or Togeri were wearing KLA patches or insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What arms were they bearing?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: 7.62 automatic weapon, short; an ammunition carrier in the belt; they were wearing military boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was Ramush Haradinaj's reaction when you told him that you were a military man, that you had graduated from the army, and that you were there to discuss about the UCK with him, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: My wish was to be in contact with them and to be engaged with the Kosovo Liberation Army, willingly, so that I could help. But I asked them if -- if there was the headquarters where my colleagues were engaged. Ramush said that we -- we know that there is some headquarter existing, but we do not recognise them, we don't much about them. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what that's about, what you just said about your colleagues and headquarters and Ramush saying, There is some existing but we don't recognise it. What was all that about?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I was thinking that there should be a general headquarters for the Kosovo Liberation Army with all the powers which would be directly engaged with the operations, but from the impression that I got there, there was no such headquarters. And there were colleagues of mine who were interested to help the war effort, and I thought that I wanted to meet them so that they could come and get in touch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your impression when you were meeting Ramush Haradinaj as to whether or not you were at KLA headquarters that first time you met him?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: My impression -- my first impression was that there was the -- the only place where people got together, but it was not a genuine headquarters in the real sense of the word. But Ramush informed me and introduced me to Togeri, who was an experienced person, he said. I did not know then that he was called Toger, but I thought that was a military title and I thought he was one of the military people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did Ramush tell you about Togeri when -- on that time when you first met him?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He said, This is Togeri, an experienced person in warfare, and that was it. It was a very short meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about Togeri's war experience, like where he had fought and for who?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: As I said earlier, he told me that his experience -- he's experienced in warfare from Croatia, from the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who did he fight for?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He had fought on the side of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you notice any rank of -- military rank on Toger's uniform?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: No, he wasn't carrying any ranks, but the word itself "Toger" made me understand that he was a career military officer; that was my impression, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What questions did Ramush Haradinaj ask you about yourself at that first meeting and your experience?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He asked me where I had studied in the military academy, and I explained that I had graduated from the military academy in Belgrade and I had studied artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was Ramush Haradinaj's overall reaction to your coming to Gllogjan and seeing him?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Very modest. It was good. That was my impression. I can't remember any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about further organisational military activity. Did you discuss anything about what your role might be with Ramush on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: No. I was interested to find out what I could do, and he said I could return to my village and try to organise people there. But the thing was that my village and the surrounding villages were not engaged yet. And I said that I could deal with the military organisation, but I had no weapons at my disposal. I was lacking in weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Ramush give you any -- I'll withdraw that. What did he say when you told him you were lacking in weaponry? What was his response to your saying that?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He said I should go back to my village and organise people there, get together some young people who could come and could go to Gllogjan, and from there they could go to Albania to get weapons. And that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you're saying "that's what I did," do you mean you went back to your village or you went to Albania? That's a little unclear.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I went back to my village. I organised the village, that's what happened. I appointed some emergency staff. Some young people, young men, turned up and reported, and I told them to go to Gllogjan, and later they went to carry some light weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You referred a little earlier to Ramush telling you the young people could go to Gllogjan and from there go to Albania to get weapons. Did any of those young men you sent go to Gllogjan go to Albania to bring back weapons?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about that? When did they go to Albania, in what circumstances? How did they get the weapons back, where did they take them to?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: As I said earlier, there was a group of young people who we appointed from the village. They went to Gllogjan. From Gllogjan, they went towards the border with Albania. They stayed for a few days. They brought back some light weapons and brought it back with them in very inconvenient circumstances at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did they pay for the weapons?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they paid, as they told me, about 300 Deutschemarks for a light weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about mortars? Were there any mortars brought back?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Later on. That happened later on. In the village then, it was only the beginning, and at the beginning it was only three, four people and they brought back some -- some weaponry. And they had a hand-held mortar, I think. As far as I can remember, it was 300-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When they came back from Albania, did they go via Gllogjan back to your village with these light automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: No. They went to Albania and they came back from different direction, from wherever they could, because the Serb forces were lined up along the border. So they chose a different route, they chose a different route into the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You described light automatic weapons. Did they have any ammunition or other types of weapons such as grenades?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: They had some ammunition, some grenades, very few. It was an outdated ammunition and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know where they got it from in Albania or under what circumstances they were able to get these weapons in Albania?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't know, but all I know is that they crossed the border into Albania. But I don't know any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: It was from the people that I heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you mean the people who went there?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: It was the people who went across the border into Albania, met some people on the other side, and it was them who provided the weapons for them. They had to get in touch with these people in Albania to get hold of the weapons that they bought.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'd like you to give the Trial Chamber a bit more detail about your organisation of the young men in the village after your first meeting with Ramush Haradinaj. What did you do and how did you organise them?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: But that was the first phase, so these young people, they travelled across to Albania to bring the weapons. And they were very daring young men who decided to join the effort in the village, and the village agreed to provide them with some money. And they also gave them some light weapons to protect themselves, and that's what happened. But that happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the connection with the KLA at the point when these young men from the village went to Albania and you were organising them in the village after your meeting with Ramush?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: No, we were not connected, but later the situation got worse. The Serbian forces had their positions set up closer and the people were in a very poor situation and surrounded. So each and every person in one form or another was trying to protect their house, the village, and the surrounding area with all they could. So after some time, the surrounding villages were organised in a similar way, so there was a new organisation in Gllogjan, and the regional staff was established in Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the KLA when you say "regional staff"?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, for the KLA. It was being established there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber about a person called Faik Gecaj from Donja Luka.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, Faik Gecaj was a village -- a villager from my village. He lived abroad, he came back. In the first meeting that we had in the village, Faik Gecaj declared that he could travel to Albania and could bring back weapons to the villages, and that's what happened. He left there, after two weeks he came back. He only knows how he organised that with the mules and horses, and he brought weapons to the village. They were simple weapons, unsophisticated, rusty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How much money did he take with him?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He did not have money, but it was organised from Albania. There were people from the village who collected money. He had a meeting with people in Albania, and we are talking about 25.000 Deutschemarks. The village agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long was it after your first meeting with Ramush Haradinaj that Faik Gecaj went to Albania to collect these weapons?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: It was a long time, because in the first phase there were four people who went and they brought back a small quantity of weapons. But Faik Gecaj went there -- he went there sometime -- a month after the meeting that I had with Ramush.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So that would make it mid-May, is that correct, mid-May 1998?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: It was around about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want you to describe to the Trial Chamber the level of organisation of the villages surrounding yours and Gllogjan by the end of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Look, it was the beginning then. The surrounding villages were being every day harassed by the Serb forces. A part of the villages were not engaged with the KLA, but each and every village had its own organisation. As I said earlier, in the similar way that I did it in the village and it's -- it expanded from then, and it was the will of the young people, in other villages some small cells were established other villages. And that brought about an expansion of the Kosovo Liberation Army in Dukagjin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Describe to the Trial Chamber the harassment by the Serb forces. Who were these forces and what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: It was the police who could come up to the villages, and they interrogated people, and there were many people who were politically involved with political parties or other things. This was the kind of harassment that the people were being subjected to. And looking at all that was going on in this respect, the village decided to get organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did your village do to get organised?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: As I said, we had a meeting. We decided to appoint some guards, night guards, and they had no weapons initially. For everything -- I told them to report to me for everything. We improvised a system through which the road -- the roads leading into and out of the village be guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have check-points or organised check-points on the road leading into your village?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that was what I said. A check-point is a big word for what we did. It was a very simple operation. There was one guard. It wasn't a check-point in the real sense, in the real military sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was this guard stopping people coming into the village or checking them or what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: The people who we knew, there was no need to stop them because people knew each other in the villages. But if there was any suspicious person approaching, we would stop him and would check his identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the guard armed or uniformed?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: No. At the beginning they were not, but later, yes. However, they were not wearing uniforms. It -- there was not enough uniforms around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I said at the beginning some of them were not, but later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was later?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: For example, in my village at the beginning in the first month we had nothing. After a month, we had some weapons and the weapons that we got hold of we -- were passed on to the guards, but there were no uniforms. The guards were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Two things here. Which month are you talking about and what weapons are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Look, at the beginning, the first month when we got organised, we had no weapons. We had no uniforms. Later on we got light weapons, semi-automatic rifles, some hand-grenades. There was a 20-millimetre gun, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In terms of the month you're referring to at the beginning, the first month, we've heard evidence about March, April, and May, 1998 so far. Which is the first month you're referring to when you got organised?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: As you are asking me, I'm talking about right from the start of the organisation of the village. That's the -- that's the first month. I can't remember the date, but I'm referring to the point when I first organised the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long after the attack by the MUP on the Haradinaj family compound did you start to organise the village?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in the village we had no weapons. It was about two weeks, two weeks after that and it took a little bit longer for the weapons to arrive, so it was probably mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A little earlier you referred to small cells being established in other villages, and then you said, And that brought about an expansion of the Kosovo Liberation Army in Dukagjin. I want you to tell the Court what you mean by "an expansion of the KLA" in Dukagjin. What happened? How did it begin to expand?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Look, the situation in Gllogjan and the surrounding villages was very serious. The Serbian forces and the Yugoslav Army forces, they were establishing their positions in key points. So almost all the villages there were surrounded and they were under the supervision of the Serb forces. And the population was in a very dire situation. So with -- based on the will of the people, every village started to form their own staffs, who joined the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a meeting organised by Ramush Haradinaj for representatives of the villages?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that happened sometime at the end of May. I do not remember the exact date. We had an invitation, all the representatives of the villages of the Dukagjin area, but it was more specific. It was the representatives of the villages around Gllogjan. So that we had an invitation to get together and we met to discuss further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P123.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I appreciate that's not the clearest thing on the screen. I have a print-out which may assist you, if you want to have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the print-out clearer, Mr. -- could I just have a look at the print-out to see whether -- Madam Usher, could you -- could we just have a look at the print-out. One second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Being the invitation that Mr. Haradinaj sent to you to attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Has that been tendered? I think it had an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is on the long list of MFI numbers. We'll deal with that soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you find out about who had prepared that particular invitation?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Later I heard that Faton Mehemetaj, who lived in Pozhare, had prepared this invitation because he had a typing machine and he had written such kind of invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he have a position within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I didn't know what kind of position he had then, but later, following the -- following this meeting on that date, I learnt about the post he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what post --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He was in charge of information. He was in charge of contacts with the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was he based?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He was based in his house, in Pozhare.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Fitnete Ramosaj, who was that?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Ramosaj, Ramosaj. Fitnete Ramosaj was a woman from a village called Carrabreg. She always lived at that time in Pozhare. I had no knowledge about the family links she had with Faton Mehemetaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did she have anything to do, as far as you were aware, with the issuing of the invitations to attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, surely she had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was her position?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Together with Faton, they worked together, and they dealt with contacts and information with various media for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying that she was also in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you go to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was the meeting held?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: The meeting took place in the village of Gllogjan, in the house of Mehemetaj, in a room. It took place at about -- in the evening, at about 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: It was a great number of people. I don't know exactly the number. They were all representatives from surrounding villages. Probably one to three representatives from each village, but I don't remember the exact number. It was a big room which was full of people. Very few of them carried uniforms. Most of them were in civilian clothes. They did not carry any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there more than 50? Less than 50? More than a hundred? Less than a hundred? Can you give an approximation of how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, they were probably more than 50 but less than 100. I don't know exactly the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who chaired the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, soon I take it you'll come to the content of the meeting. I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps it would be a better idea to start that, but if there's any other introductory -- then, Mr. Tetaj, we'll have a break for 25 minutes. So we'll resume at 20 minutes past 4.00. Before we do so, Mr. Re, I received a message that the original estimate of three and a half hours would be reduced to one and a half hours in view of 92 ter. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The message didn't come from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll verify where it comes from. How much --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think it comes via a conversation I had with Mr. Emmerson this morning. I would think probably another hour. I think I've been going for an hour and ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, fine. We'll resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I first will apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The apologies have already been accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Had received the message, and provisionally the message that had come back was that Your Honour had been kind enough to indicate that I could begin my cross-examination in the morning, which I'm grateful for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll have an opportunity to read the transcript and start your cross-examination in the morning. We'll resume until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you may proceed. But I'd first like to address you, Mr. Tetaj. I see that you've got some papers in front of you. If at any moment you'd like to consult these papers, would you, please, first address me and tell me what the papers are and why you'd like to consult them at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the same, the same thing which you gave to me, and this was the invitation you sent to me to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was written here. You can ask me any question you want. I'll try to answer them as well as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When I indicated an hour before, I might have been slightly optimistic, but I'll certainly finish well within the time indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, just before the break we were talking about the meeting that Mr. Haradinaj chaired, held at the house of Mehemetaj in Gllogjan. My first question to you is: Why was it held in that particular house?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Look, I don't know the reason why. I only know that -- the main reason was that the Serb forces -- the Serb forces had reached up to Gllogjan. So Gllogjan was in a sort of -- in a circle surrounded by the Serb forces. I don't know if there is any particular reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did Mr. Haradinaj chair the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Mr. Haradinaj was from Gllogjan. He -- his compound was once attacked. His family was attacked. He protected his compound, and then his village was also attacked. So probably these were the reasons why. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know who organised the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: According to the invitation, the meeting was considered necessary so that all the leaders of the villages could sit down and discuss some of the current situation as well as the current developments at the time. Therefore, this meeting was called to take place in Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know who was the person responsible for organising or calling the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: This was initiative of everybody who was present there, according to the invitation Ramush and Mehemetaj were indeed the people who had initiated the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were minutes taken of the my colleague?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. First Ramush addressed the meeting. He talked about the current situation at the time in Gllogjan and in surrounding areas. He talked about Dukagjin in the narrow sense of the region. Then also -- and also the minutes were written down at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a person there called Kompjuteri.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there was a person nicknamed Kompjuteri. He was the person who took the minutes. I have not seen the minutes. I don't know what was written there. I don't know the content of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's Kompjuteri's name? Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Very late I learned about that, after a very long period of time. I learned that Kompjuteri was Emrush Xhemajli.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From where? Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: From Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was he wearing at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He was wearing a uniform, a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Togeri there?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Togeri took part. He disappeared once and then I didn't see him any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He was present very, very briefly. I saw him only once and then I didn't see him any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Probably civilian clothes in dark colour, not camouflaged uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Ramush, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Ramush was wearing camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he tell the meeting about the current situation at the time in Gllogjan and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He informed everybody that the situation was difficult. The situation was, indeed, very difficult. He told the participants that we were all surrounded by the Serbs and that all the roads which linked this area to Decane and Gjakove, they were roads on which there was big movement of columns with heavy equipment of the Serbian army. The Serbs had taken positions on most of the key positions in the region, Suka and Baballoq. So the situation was difficult. Therefore, Ramush, speaking in cold-bloodedness, asked the participants to defend their villages, to be aware of the situation, to be mature, and to know what they should do. So this is the things about which he talked to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did he speak for?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: He spoke for a very long time, and then -- we also waited, in fact, for a long time until everybody came together, but I don't remember exactly how long he talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "a long time," are you measuring it in hours?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in terms of hours. So that began after 8.00, 9.00 in the evening. Yes, yes, I'm talking about hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he tell the meeting about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, he talked about the founding of the army. He said it was time to coordinate all the villages at that particular moment. He said that -- that everybody -- that we should set up a kind of structure, a kind of something which would command the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was proposed to be the overall commander?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Look, the idea was that Gllogjan should be a subordinate area. So I proposed at the meeting that the area should be divided into subareas on basis of village. So I proposed that four subareas should be set up. Ramush and the others accepted this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your proposal?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: I couldn't understand your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You proposed four subareas being set up. What were those four subareas that you proposed being set up?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I was present and I proposed that the area in Dukagjin should be divided into subareas. I also said that people of military experience should be put in command. I proposed the establishment of zone number 1 with Gllogjan; then zone number 2 should be Irzniq; zone number 3 should be Pozhare; and zone 4 should be the area which was divided by river of Bistrica as well as the villages of Isniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go to zone number 1, who was to be the commander of zone number 1, which was Gllogjan? Just the name, please.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: It was decided that zone number 1, since this was Gllogjan, Ramush Haradinaj, the commander of this zone, should be the commander. Then Shemsedin Ceku was proposed to be the commander of zone 2, somebody -- he was a person with military experience. Zone number 3 should be under my command. And then zone number 4, which was more extensive, should be placed under the command of Skender Rexhahmetaj and Gani Gjukaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you -- Mr. Tetaj, please listen carefully to the question. I just want to take you to each zone one by one. The first one was zone 1, Gllogjan and Ramush Haradinaj --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, subdivision, subarea, that's how we called it. The whole zone was considered Dukagjini Plain. The proposal was that this place should be decided into subzones, subareas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the physical boundaries of the Dukagjini Plain area?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Dukagjin area?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: You're talking about Dukagjin or about the subareas and the villages which belong to these subareas?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I wonder whether if Mr. Re is going to invite the witness to indicate the boundaries of the collection of territory covered by these four subzones, whether it might assist us all to have a map in front of us so the witness can give an indication exactly what it is he's talking about, given the precise territorial issue may be of some importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also, perhaps, Mr. Re, we could be very precise on what I think was at one moment called the Dukagjin Plain or -- well, at least there was another word which we find already in the statements of the witness. So the -- that there's no confusion whatsoever about what you asked him as far as the Dukagjin Zone is concerned -- I see it's the Dukagjin Plain in 41, line 7. Perhaps map 10 would do and then ask the witness perhaps to draw a line around the whole of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's actually the larger one I require --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- and we could take an exact of that area. D32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D32. Madam Registrar, could you please put D32 on the screen. Nevertheless, I take it that some zooming-in could be done, Mr. Re, because otherwise, it's very large and it might be not so easy. You know that zooming it later is not possible under the same number anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It may be safer to give him A3 print-out and have him mark on that, although I do understand e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this -- would this do as we have it here or would a more limited area do as well, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, can you see the map clearly on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, but it's very small. Nevertheless, I will indicate the boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that map big enough to show the entirety of the Dukagjin Plain or area or do you need a larger map?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again, Mr. Re what the issue is here, and the question that the witness needs to be invited to address his mind to is the territory covered by the four subzones that came together, and if we keep slipping between that territory and concept about the Dukagjin Plain, knowing what we know about the witness's evidence as to what took place later on, it's bound to confuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't understand the objection. I'm asking the witness to look at the four subzones, which are in the larger ones, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if we start with the four subzones and ask the witness to mark the subzones on the map and then you could ask him or in cross-examination you could ask him whether these four subzones, whether -- what that would be taken together. Witness, is the map clear enough for you at this moment to identify the four subzones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see only a part, not the whole. It's interrupted exactly at my village. Gllogjan is not here. It should have been here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We have to zoom out. We have certainly to zoom out. Now to zoom in a bit. Move a bit up to the north. Can you orient yourself on this part of the map as it is now and just to -- just to assist you -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could be of some assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we take Peje and move it as far up as we can, I think it may be of some assistance in terms of the area that the witness is speaking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have to identify the exact portion of the map. We can't move that later on, move -- zooming in, zooming out as the witness marks the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't read it myself, Your Honour. We have some hard copies being printed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- and brought down, maybe if I come back to it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- ask the witness to -- how many hard copy do you have, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have four coming down, but he only needs one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I take it that we'll invite the witness to mark it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could make another suggestion, because I myself on my personal map dealing with this same issue, I marked each of the subzones in a different colour and it may be some assistance to the Chamber at a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You even could suggest to Mr. Re that if your subzones are the same as his subzones, to show it to him and if you would agree on the matter, ask the witness to confirm that. That might be a practical way of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, can you please assist Mr. Guy-Smith in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's fairly rough. I'd actually prefer to show the witness and ask him just to draw on the map. I'm not in any way disputing what Mr. Guy-Smith is saying are the areas, but it's colour-coded in a way which may not necessarily be of assistance to the Court as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it if Madam Usher returns the map to Mr. Guy-Smith and let's hope that we get a less-rough marking. Then, Madam Usher, could you put the map on the ELMO so that everyone can follow. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If it's of any assistance, certainly I would have no objection if Mr. Re were to lead the villages that the witness has referred to in paragraphs 44 and 45 of the consolidated witness statement. I'm not sure which paragraphs they are in the 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid they're not --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They're not in the 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But the villages are there spelled out for each subzone. Paragraph 44 deals with subzone 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean that Mr. Re leads the witness in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And put those villages to the witness specifically and then -- and that will help us to mark up the boundaries of the zones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, a lot of help from many Defence teams. Take advantage if you can have any advantage from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm indebted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, zone 1, according to your statement, was the village of Gllogjan, Shaptej, Gramocelj, Dubrava, Babaloc, Prilep, and Rastavica, can you please mark those villages on as number -- those within zone number 1.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: So we're talking about the subzone, subzone number 1, because you mentioned the word "zone." Zone is something bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: These were all four subzones.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'd just like you to mark them on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Subzone number 1 of Gllogjan, it included Gllogjan, Shaptej, Dubrava, Baballoq, Prilep, Rastovice --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: These were the areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to mark them, physically mark them on the map. Can you draw a circle around the area which is subzone 1 and just put a cross on the villages, please.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Oh, oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just do a circle around the subzone, put a 1 in it --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Okay, okay, I understood you now. I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Next one is number 2, which according to your statement, was Rznic, Gornji, Donji Ratis, Beleg, and Kodralija.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ
utterances.text: Irzniq, Ratishe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
